should have been taken, they instead took <term>pyrite</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials in which there is no operation; these are expensive things from the shops, yet in the labor they are of no value at all. Our matter, however, is bought from no shop; nevertheless, it is found daily, and merchants cast it out into the streets. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the matter of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>the Philosophers' Stone</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor: for our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite other things of that kind. Yet it is not dug out of the wild and rural mountains with hammers and other instruments. Our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs: in our <term>Salt-spring</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found: from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are smelted, and not from the wild, foreign, and rural mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them; for the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses. For this reason, they employed these things otherwise than was proper, and did not aim at the mark at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads; for instance, while they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> <gloss>heated to vapor</gloss> with a strong fire; they scorched with <term>strong waters</term> <gloss>corrosive acids</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, when they should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> there, and again, like men unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and, with lying words, kept saying that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they themselves are deservedly lying: for their own ignorance shamefully deceived them. This must be imputed to their own obscure and murky cunning, while, according to their own dark intellect, they interpreted the words differently than they sounded. For example, while the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pretenders to philosophy</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced the things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Also, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <note>original: "nasutuli", literally "those with big noses", meaning people who think they are clever or superior</note> burned nature with <term>strong water</term>, and with that same water, which has no

<summary>The author distinguishes between the common materials used by failed alchemists and the true, free "matter" of the Philosophers. He criticizes "Philosophasters" for misinterpreting alchemical terms and using excessive heat or acids that destroy the work.</summary>
<keywords>alchemical matter, salt, mercury, sulfur, distillation, calcination, Philosophasters, strong water, corrosive acids</keywords>
